                                    PROJECT NO. 58481


 LARGE LOAD                                 §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS                  §                        OF TEXAS
                                            §


Introduction

       The City of Red Oak appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Commission’s
questions regarding the proposed Large Load Interconnection framework under SB 6. Our
comments align financial risk with planning certainty and preserve the viability of
economically sound projects.

       Red Oak is a city of approximately 20,000 residents located along I-35E, 18 miles
south of downtown Dallas. For more than 25 years, the City has pursued a deliberate
strategy of land assembly and industrial recruitment to strengthen and diversify its tax
base. Early successes included attracting Triumph Aerospace (now Qarbon Aerospace)
and Bombardier Aviation.

        In recent years, Red Oak has become a hub for hyperscale data center
development. The City currently has three hyperscale data center campuses under
construction, permitted by the City, with land acquired and energization approvals in
place. Two of the three campuses are already partially operational. Together, these
projects represent more than $11 billion in capital investment, nearly four times the City’s
total taxable value of $2.86 billion in 2025.

       Despite this success, additional projects remain stalled due to uncertainty around
electric service. Red Oak has three additional hyperscale data center projects,
representing approximately $11 billion in investment. These projects have paid millions of
dollars in deposits to the interconnecting utility and yet do not have line of sight to electric
service commitments from the utility. In addition, a separate $15 billion data center
project located outside Oncor’s service territory has received only a partial power
commitment and still requires additional service to proceed.

        The stakes are significant. Over the past six months, Red Oak lost two projects
totaling $7 billion in investment because developers grew frustrated with the lack of a
clear, timely, and transparent process for receiving power commitments. The City


                                                1
 therefore strongly supports rules that provide certainty, transparency, and predictability in
a high-growth environment.

      We offer the following targeted recommendations to improve the clarity and
operability of the proposed rule.

Discussion Draft Suggested Changes

   1. Improve transparency and milestone-based communication.
      Large load customers often have limited visibility into study progress even after
      paying required fees. While the draft requires notice upon completion of the Large
      Load Interconnection Study (LLIS), it does not require interim updates. Red Oak
      recommends requiring utility communications when:

          o   an LLI number is assigned,
          o   the LLIS kick-off meeting is scheduled,
          o   material study milestones in the LLIS are reached,
          o   the Load Commissioning Plan (LCP) is updated, and
          o   scope changes are requested by ERCOT or neighboring TSPs.

   2. Set reasonable interim security requirements.
      Red Oak supports interim agreement security in the range of $20,000–$28,000 per
      MW. Multiple stakeholders have broadly opposed flat, high early-stage security
      requirements because they are misaligned with system cost risk. While some
      projects may be able to support $100,000 per MW, that level should not be the
      default. A more proportionate security posted at interim agreement execution,
      which is signed before the LLIS begins, will ensure that viable projects are not
      unnecessarily excluded.

   3. Align financial commitments with planning certainty.
      Financial commitments should escalate as information improves. The current draft
      requires significant commitments before studies identify defined upgrades or costs.
      Early-stage security should remain refundable while uncertainty is high. As studies
      progress and impacts become clearer, commitments can appropriately become
      non-refundable. Once project-specific facilities are defined, customers should
      transition to CIAC, consistent with existing practice. This sequencing aligns risk with
      information availability and avoids front-loading costs prematurely.



                                              2
    4. Clarify non-retroactivity.
      The rule should clearly state that new financial commitment requirements do not
      apply retroactively to projects that have already executed an interconnection
      agreement and will have satisfied financial obligations within six months of the
      effective date of the rule. Applying new requirements to materially advanced
      projects would create unnecessary uncertainty and undermine settled
      expectations.

   5. Remove operational standards from the interconnection rule.
      Interconnection requirements and operational standards serve distinct purposes.
      Operational standards are more appropriately addressed in protocols or operating
      guides. Combining them in a single rule risks confusion and unnecessary
      gatekeeping.

   The City of Red Oak respectfully urges the Commission to adopt clear, functional rules
that provide regulatory certainty consistent with SB 6 and responsive to the scale and
urgency of load growth in ERCOT. Our community cannot afford to lose transformative
investment due to avoidable uncertainty or procedural friction. We appreciate the
Commission’s consideration of these comments.


                                  Respectfully Submitted,

                                         Dr. Mark Stanfill
                                         Mayor, City of Red Oak




                                            3
                                 PROJECT NO. 58481
                   Executive Summary of City of Red Oak Comments

       The City of Red Oak appreciates the opportunity to comment on Project 58481. The
City supports a framework that aligns financial commitments with planning certainty and
provides transparency throughout the interconnection process. Red Oak is a rapidly
growing community south of Dallas that has become a hub for hyperscale data center
investment with more than $11 billion currently under construction and over $25 billion in
additional projects constrained by uncertainty. The City has also experienced the loss of
prospective investments due to the absence of clear, timely path to power, underscoring
the need for rules that provide regulatory certainty. Our suggestions are as follows:

   1. Improve transparency and communication. The rule should require milestone-
      based communications, including assignment of an LLI number, scheduling of LLIS
      kick-off meetings, achievement of material study milestones, updates to the Load
      Commissioning Plan, and requests for scope changes and restudies.

   2. Set reasonable early-stage financial security requirements. Red Oak supports
      interim agreement security in the range of $20,000–$28,000 per MW.

   3. Align financial commitments with planning certainty. Financial commitments
      should escalate as system impacts and costs become better defined. Early-stage
      security should remain refundable while uncertainty is high. As studies progress,
      commitments may appropriately become non-refundable.

   4. Avoid retroactive application of new requirements. New financial commitment
      requirements should not apply to projects that have already executed
      interconnection agreements and that will satisfy financial obligations within six
      months of the rule’s effective date.

   5. Remove operational standards from the interconnection rule. Interconnection
      requirements and operational standards serve different purposes and should be
      addressed separately to avoid confusion and unnecessary gatekeeping.

       The City of Red Oak respectfully urges the Commission to adopt a Large Load
Interconnection framework that delivers regulatory certainty, supports orderly system
planning, and enables transformative investment to proceed in ERCOT’s high-growth
environment.
